questiontext.text: In a B+ tree, where do the actual records / data values reside?

answer.text: Only in the leaf nodes

feedback.text: Correct — all data lives in the leaves; internal nodes hold only routing keys.

answer.text: Only in the root node

feedback.text: The root is just an internal router, not a data store.

answer.text: In both internal and leaf nodes

feedback.text: That describes a classic B-tree; a B+ tree confines data to leaves.

answer.text: In a separate hash table

feedback.text: No — the data is held in the leaf level of the tree itself.

generalfeedback.text: A B+ tree separates navigation from storage: internal nodes route, leaves store.

questiontext.text: What role do the internal nodes of a B+ tree play?

answer.text: They hold keys only, acting as routers (separators) that guide the search downward

feedback.text: Correct — internal keys are separator copies, not data.

answer.text: They store the full data records

feedback.text: No — records live only in the leaves.

answer.text: They link horizontally to support range scans

feedback.text: It is the leaves that are linked, not the internal nodes.

answer.text: They are always empty until a delete occurs

feedback.text: Internal nodes always carry separator keys.

generalfeedback.text: Because internal nodes carry no data, they pack more separator keys per block, raising fan-out.

questiontext.text: Which structural feature makes B+ tree range and in-order scans especially fast?

answer.text: The leaves are linked together in a sorted list

feedback.text: Correct — after finding the start, you walk the leaf links sequentially.

answer.text: Every key is hashed for O(1) lookup

feedback.text: B+ trees are ordered, not hashed; hashing would break range order.

answer.text: Data is duplicated in every internal node

feedback.text: Internal nodes hold only routing keys, no data.

answer.text: The tree re-sorts itself on each query

feedback.text: No re-sorting occurs; order is maintained by structure.

generalfeedback.text: The linked leaf list turns a range query into one descent plus a sequential walk — ideal for databases.

questiontext.text: Compared with a B-tree of the same block size, why does a B+ tree tend to be shorter?

answer.text: Internal nodes store no data, so each block packs more keys, raising fan-out

feedback.text: Correct — higher fan-out means fewer levels for the same key count.

answer.text: It removes duplicate keys entirely

feedback.text: Separator keys are actually duplicated into internal nodes.

answer.text: It uses binary nodes instead of multiway nodes

feedback.text: It is a multiway structure, like the B-tree.

answer.text: It stores everything in the root

feedback.text: Data is in the leaves, spread across the leaf level.

generalfeedback.text: Data-free internal nodes maximize branching factor, shrinking tree height and I/O per lookup.

questiontext.text: In a B+ tree the leaf nodes are chained together so they can be traversed as a sorted sequential list.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — the linked leaves enable fast sequential and range access.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Leaf linkage is a defining feature of the B+ tree.

questiontext.text: In a B+ tree the internal nodes store full data records alongside their keys.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — internal nodes hold only separator keys; data lives in the leaves.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — internal nodes route only; the records are all in the leaves.

questiontext.text: The B+ tree is the standard on-disk ______ structure used by relational databases and filesystems. (one English word)

answer.text: index

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: index*

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: indexing

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements distinguishing a B+ tree from a B-tree are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: A B+ tree keeps all data records in the leaves; a B-tree keeps data in internal nodes too

feedback.text: Yes — this is the core structural difference.

answer.text: A B+ tree links its leaves for fast range scans; a plain B-tree does not

feedback.text: Yes — linked leaves are a B+ tree feature.

answer.text: A B+ tree is unbalanced while a B-tree is balanced

feedback.text: No — both are height-balanced with all leaves at equal depth.

answer.text: A B+ tree has lower fan-out than a B-tree of the same block size

feedback.text: No — data-free internal nodes give a B+ tree higher fan-out.

generalfeedback.text: B+ trees confine data to linked leaves and gain higher fan-out; both trees remain balanced.
